subject: bio
title: Cell Membranes
subtitle: Fluid mosaic model, membrane transport and osmosis.
concept: The fluid mosaic model describes the cell membrane as a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that move laterally.
Molecules cross membranes by passive transport (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis) or active transport — the last requires ATP.
Osmosis is the movement of water by diffusion through a partially permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential.

notes.heading: The Fluid Mosaic Model
items: The cell surface membrane is described by the fluid mosaic model: a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that can move laterally (fluid), and a variety of protein types scattered throughout (mosaic).

Intrinsic (integral) proteins span the bilayer — they include channel proteins (allow specific ions/small molecules through by facilitated diffusion) and carrier proteins (change shape to transport molecules, can be active or passive). Extrinsic (peripheral) proteins sit on the surface and are often involved in cell signalling.

Cholesterol molecules intercalate between the fatty acid tails — they prevent the membrane becoming too fluid at high temperatures and too rigid at low temperatures, stabilising fluidity across a range of conditions.

Glycoproteins and glycolipids have carbohydrate chains on the outer surface — they act as receptors for hormones and neurotransmitters, cell-surface antigens for immune recognition, and adhesion molecules.

notes.heading: Membrane Transport
items: Simple diffusion: small, non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂, lipid-soluble substances) dissolve directly into and pass through the lipid bilayer, moving down their concentration gradient. No proteins or energy required.

Facilitated diffusion: polar or charged molecules (glucose, ions) cannot cross the bilayer directly — they move down their concentration gradient through specific channel or carrier proteins. Passive — no ATP required.

Active transport: molecules move against their concentration gradient through carrier proteins, driven by ATP hydrolysis (ATP → ADP + Pᵢ). The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is the classic example — pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP molecule.
Bulk transport: endocytosis (membrane engulfs material to form a vesicle inside the cell) and exocytosis (vesicle fuses with membrane to release contents outside) transport large molecules.

notes.heading: Osmosis and Water Potential
items: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules by diffusion through a partially permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential (Ψ) to a region of lower water potential.

Pure water has Ψ = 0 (the maximum possible). Dissolving solutes lowers Ψ — the more concentrated the solution, the more negative (lower) its water potential. Water always moves from less negative to more negative Ψ.

In animal cells: a hypertonic external solution (lower Ψ) draws water out → crenation (cell shrinks). A hypotonic solution (higher Ψ) drives water in → lysis (cell bursts) because there is no cell wall.

In plant cells: hypertonic solution causes plasmolysis — the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall. A hypotonic solution makes the cell turgid — the cell wall exerts wall pressure, preventing lysis.

definitions.body: The model of membrane structure in which phospholipids form a bilayer with embedded proteins; both lipids and proteins can move laterally.
The net movement of water molecules by diffusion from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
A measure of the tendency of water to move; pure water = 0; more negative = lower water potential; water moves from less negative to more negative Ψ.
Movement of molecules against a concentration gradient across a membrane, requiring ATP and carrier proteins.
The shrinkage of plant cell contents away from the cell wall when the cell is placed in a hypertonic solution.

workedExamples.q: Explain why a red blood cell bursts when placed in distilled water.

steps.text: Distilled water has Ψ = 0; the cell contents have a lower (more negative) Ψ due to dissolved solutes.
Water moves by osmosis down the Ψ gradient into the cell through the partially permeable membrane.
The cell swells; animal cells have no cell wall to resist pressure, so the membrane bursts (lysis/haemolysis).

mistakes: Describing osmosis as 'water moving from high to low concentration' — use water potential terminology: 'from high to low water potential'.
Confusing channel proteins (water/ions, passive) with carrier proteins (larger molecules, passive or active).
Stating that active transport uses 'energy' without specifying ATP.
tips: Water always moves from less negative (higher) to more negative (lower) Ψ.
Remember: cholesterol increases rigidity at high T and prevents rigidity at low T — it buffers fluidity.
In exam answers, state direction of movement AND the type of transport for full marks.

flashcards.q: What is the function of cholesterol in the cell membrane?
flashcards.a: Regulates membrane fluidity — prevents excessive fluidity at high temperatures and excessive rigidity at low temperatures.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between channel and carrier proteins?
flashcards.a: Channel proteins form pores for ions/water (passive only). Carrier proteins change shape to transport specific molecules (passive or active).
A measure of the tendency of water to move; pure water = 0; solutions have negative Ψ. Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) Ψ.
When a plant cell is in a hypertonic solution, water leaves by osmosis and the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall.

flashcards.q: Name two roles of glycoproteins in the cell membrane.
flashcards.a: Cell signalling / hormone receptor; cell recognition; immune response (any 2).

flashcards.q: How does active transport differ from facilitated diffusion?
flashcards.a: Active transport moves molecules AGAINST the concentration gradient and requires ATP; facilitated diffusion is passive (down the gradient, no ATP).

questions.q: Which molecules pass through the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion?
questions.exp: Small non-polar molecules like O₂ and CO₂ dissolve in and pass directly through the lipid bilayer.

questions.q: A cell is placed in a solution with lower water potential than its cytoplasm. What happens?
questions.exp: Water moves by osmosis from higher Ψ (cell) to lower Ψ (solution) — water leaves the cell.

questions.q: What is the role of cholesterol in the membrane?
questions.exp: Cholesterol sits between fatty acid tails, preventing them packing too closely or being too fluid — it stabilises fluidity.

questions.q: Active transport requires which of the following?
questions.exp: Active transport moves molecules against the gradient; this requires ATP (hydrolysed to ADP + Pᵢ) and specific carrier proteins.

questions.q: What is the fluid mosaic model?
opts: Membrane is a rigid layer of proteins
Phospholipid bilayer with mobile embedded proteins
Single layer of lipids with fixed proteins
questions.exp: The fluid mosaic model: phospholipid bilayer with proteins that can move laterally within the bilayer (fluid = mobile; mosaic = variety of proteins).

recall: Explain the difference between simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport.
Define water potential and explain the direction of osmosis.
Explain why plant cells do not burst in hypotonic solutions.
State the role of glycoproteins and cholesterol in the membrane.
